What changed in the current release. The version this guide was built for is shown in the footer.
Session journal: complete under load, smaller on diskKTPH000

KTPH000A server flood can no longer punch holes into the journalKTPH001 — when output arrived faster than the capture log could persist it, up to 10,000 queued lines were silently dropped with nothing in the journal to show for it. The capture now applies backpressure instead: the terminal may briefly slow down under an extreme flood, but every line lands in the log. The log writer also batches its disk writes, so it keeps up with far more output in the first place.

KTPH002Repeated output lines are coalescedKTPH003 — progress loops, KTPH000 repeats and similar floods are stored syslog-style: the first occurrence immediately, follow-ups as one entry with a repeat count. The KTPH004journal pageKTPH005 shows such a run compactly as KTPH001; copying the log reproduces the original lines in full, and the AI summarizer sees the count instead of thousands of identical lines.

KTPH003Rotated log parts are now zstd-compressedKTPH004 — finished capture-log parts compress to KTPH000 instead of KTPH001, which is both faster and noticeably smaller on repetitive terminal output. Journals recorded by earlier versions keep their KTPH002 parts and open, export and redact exactly as before — even mixed within one journal.

KTPH001Log rotation is configurable per connectionKTPH002 — the Journal tab gained KTPH003Maximum size per log part (MB)KTPH004 (default 25) and KTPH005Maximum rotated log partsKTPH006 (default 20). Previously both were fixed, and a long noisy session simply stopped recording output after 20 parts. An enterprise policy can cap the part count with the new KTPH000 key.
Session journal: AI search and QKTPH001AKTPH000

KTPH000Ask the AI about a recorded sessionKTPH001 — the viewer's new KTPH002AI QKTPH008A panelKTPH003 answers questions like KTPH004"Were screenshots taken that show errors from this script?"KTPH005 from what the journal already collected (summaries, screenshot analyses, notes) — the raw capture log is never sent to a model. When a question needs hard evidence, the model names literal search strings, korTTY's own streaming search scans the log, and only match counts plus a few sample lines go back for the final answer. Answers cite their sources: clicking a source scrolls the timeline to the entry, clicking a log-evidence line opens the log panel scrolled to the very line. Follow-up questions continue the conversation, and KTPH006Save as noteKTPH007 appends a QKTPH009A pair to the timeline.

KTPH000One question across all journalsKTPH001 — the manager's new KTPH002AI searchKTPH003 answers questions like KTPH004"In which journals did result_complex.pl exit with an error?"KTPH005: a fast local ranking over the journals' collected entries picks the candidates, one AI request writes the summary and selects the relevant journals, and the exact hits are materialized by the internal search. The hit tree jumps straight to the entry or log line, already-opened hits stay marked across searches and restarts, the table shows a sorted KTPH006HitsKTPH007 column with a row highlight instead of filtering, and KTPH008Selection onlyKTPH009 restricts the scope. Without a reachable model the search degrades to the pure text search with a notice. Optional KTPH010Semantic journal searchKTPH011 adds embedding-based ranking when a local embedding model is configured in the knowledge stores.

KTPH000Journals now carry AI keywordsKTPH001 — the closing session summary extracts up to twelve verbatim search terms (hostnames, script and file names, error classes) into the journal metadata; the manager's filter matches them and shows them as clickable KTPH002keyword chipsKTPH003 under the filter field.
KTPH000Catch up summariesKTPH001 — the journal options can now run the summarizer over closed journals that were never summarized, one by one behind a cancellable progress dialog.

KTPH000The manager's content search reads logs streamingKTPH001 — KTPH002Search contentsKTPH003 no longer decompresses whole capture logs into memory; parts are scanned line by line, so searching across many large journals stays lightweight.
KTPH001New policy key KTPH000KTPH002 — an organization can forbid the on-demand AI over journal content (QKTPH003A panel and cross-journal AI search) while keeping AI summaries.

KTPH002A lost connection no longer closes the tabKTPH003 — when an established SSH connection drops (network outage, VPN cut, server gone), the tab now stays open in a red KTPH000 state with a red status bar showing when the connection was lost, instead of silently closing as if you had typed KTPH001. Reconnect in place with a double-click on the bar or tab, or via KTPH004ReconnectKTPH005 in the context menus; a normal remote logout still closes the tab as before.

KTPH001Connection loss is detected within about ten secondsKTPH002 — korTTY actively probes the server over the SSH connection (the same technique as OpenSSH's KTPH000) and treats two consecutive unanswered probes as a lost connection, instead of waiting minutes for a TCP timeout. The terminal cursor also stops blinking in a disconnected tab, so a dead session no longer looks alive.

KTPH000Automatic reconnectKTPH001 — a new KTPH002Settings → Terminal → Automatically reconnect lost connectionsKTPH003 option (on by default) reconnects a lost tab on its own, with delays growing from 3 seconds up to one attempt per minute and a countdown in the red status bar. Permanent failures such as a wrong password, a changed host key, or a configuration refusal are never retried automatically, and while a session journal is deciding how to continue, the journal's own reconnect choice takes precedence. See KTPH004Terminal sessions → Connection lossKTPH005.

KTPH001Removed KTPH000, an abandoned dependency with an unpatched signature-malleability flawKTPH002 (CVE-2020-36843) — Ed25519 SSH host keys and key-based authentication are now served by BouncyCastle, already part of korTTY, with no user-visible change in behavior.

KTPH001A failed connection to a host on your local network now explains itselfKTPH002 — since macOS 15, a missing Local Network permission makes any local connection fail exactly like a powered-off host (KTPH000), with nothing pointing at the actual cause. korTTY now adds a hint naming the permission when the failure and the network shape match, without ruling out a genuine outage.

Only the current release is listed here, so the guide stays short in every language it is translated into. Every version is on the KTPH002GitHub releases pageKTPH003; the curated notes for earlier versions are kept in the repository, in KTPH000 and KTPH001.
